C002.subject: scaling of current neural network architectures
C002.object: within 20 years, given continued growth in compute and data
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: scaling of current neural network architectures within 20 years, given continued growth in compute and data]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term tracking of benchmark saturation rates across diverse tasks (e.g., BIG-bench, MMLU, ARC) as model scale increases — If scaling laws hold, performance on these benchmarks should continue to improve without plateauing; evidence of a ceiling would refute the hypothesis.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of representational capacity limits in transformers (e.g., circuit complexity bounds, depth-width tradeoffs) — Formal proofs of computational bottlenecks in current architectures (e.g., inability to solve certain reasoning tasks beyond a certain scale) would provide a hard ceiling, refuting the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of historical scaling trends in neural language models and vision transformers, extrapolating to AGI-relevant metrics (e.g., reasoning, generalization, transfer learning) — Systematic review of published scaling studies can reveal whether progress is accelerating, linear, or saturating, informing the likelihood of reaching AGI within 20 years.

qualifier.tension: assumes no hard ceiling on performance from current paradigms

C005.subject: fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs
C005.object: even with aggressive scaling, within 20 years
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: fundamental algorithmic breakthroughs even with aggressive scaling, within 20 years]

[PATH:empirical] Scaling laws benchmarks on reasoning tasks (e.g., MATH, GSM8K, ARC) for models up to 10^26 FLOPs, extrapolating performance trends via parametric fits — If scaling alone yields diminishing returns on complex reasoning tasks, this would support the hypothesis that algorithmic breakthroughs are necessary; if performance continues to improve log-linearly, it would refute the plateau claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical analysis of computational complexity of AGI-relevant tasks (e.g., planning, common-sense reasoning) relative to transformer expressiveness (e.g., circuit complexity bounds, TC0 vs. P) — Proving that current architectures cannot solve certain reasoning problems within polynomial resources under scaling would confirm the need for new algorithms; conversely, showing equivalence would refute it.

[PATH:literature] Survey of historical AI scaling plateau events (e.g., symbolic AI in 1980s, deep learning in 2010s) and the algorithmic innovations that broke them (e.g., backpropagation, attention) — Identifying patterns of algorithmic necessity across past plateaus provides inductive evidence for whether current scaling can avoid a similar stagnation within 20 years.

qualifier.tension: counters the sufficiency of scaling alone; implies current trends may hit a plateau

C008.subject: AGI within 20 years under aggressive scaling
C008.object: whether current scaling laws can overcome remaining conceptual bottlenecks without novel algorithmic insights
evidence_refs: [SYNTHESIS] The apparent contradiction dissolves when we recognize that both branches capture plausible outcomes under different assumptions about the nature of remaining challenges. Branch A assumes that scaling alone will suffice to bridge gaps in reasoning, generalization, and efficiency, while Branch B assumes these gaps require fundamental algorithmic innovations. The refined claim integrates both by acknowledging that the necessity of algorithmic breakthroughs is contingent on the degree to which current architectures and scaling methods can be extended. This framing shifts the debate from a binary to a conditional question, making the contradiction productive for guiding research priorities.

qualifier.tension: counters the sufficiency of scaling alone; implies current trends may hit a plateau
